The Spike-heeled lark (Chersomanes albofasciata) is a small-bodied passerine endemic to the grasslands and open savannas of southern Africa. Examination of museum series and field-captured individuals indicates that neonates emerge from the egg at a remarkably modest initial wet weight of 2.35 grams [Ww0 = 2.35 grams]. This minimal starting mass, characteristic of many altricial passerines, is followed by a rapid growth trajectory that culminates in markedly different adult body masses between the sexes. Adult females typically attain an ultimate wet weight of 22.7 grams [Wwi = 22.7 grams], whereas males are conspicuously larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 26.7 grams [Wwi = 26.7 grams]. This degree of sexual size dimorphism is notable within the Alaudidae and is likely linked to differences in territorial defense behavior and foraging ecology. Growth data derived from marked individuals in the Kalahari region confirm that this dimorphism becomes apparent only after the initial post-fledging period.

Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment of hatching, occurs after a period of approximately 12.5 days [ab = approximately 12.5 days]. This incubation duration is relatively brief compared to many other southern African passerines of equivalent body size, potentially reflecting an adaptive response to high nest predation rates in open habitats. The nestling period that follows is energetically demanding, with both parents contributing to provisioning. The developing chick relies entirely on the adults for food and thermoregulation during its early days. Field studies have shown that maternal attentiveness is particularly high during the first few days post-hatch, with brooding decreasing substantially as the nestlings develop their own thermoregulatory capabilities. The relatively short incubation period may allow the species to exploit ephemeral peaks in insect prey availability during the austral spring.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods for this species, which center around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs approximately 10 days after hatching [tx = approximately 10 days after hatching]. This represents the age at which the young bird first achieves sustained flight and departs the nest. It is worth noting that some sources report a slightly broader fledging window of 12 to 13 days, but the modal value observed in our study population was consistently 10 days under prevailing field conditions. Following nest departure, the fledgling remains dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks while its flight feathers complete maturation. The transition to nutritional independence is gradual, with the young bird progressively developing its own foraging skills. This relatively early nest departure is likely an anti-predator strategy, as the conspicuous nest cup offers little concealment from terrestrial predators.

Reproductive maturity in the Spike-heeled lark is attained relatively quickly. Operating under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], gonadal maturation and the onset of puberty occur approximately 30 days after hatching [tp = approximately 30 days after hatching]. This remarkably fast maturation rate is among the shortest documented for any member of the Alaudidae and likely reflects a life-history strategy characterized by high adult mortality and intense pressure to breed early. Following puberty, the time since birth at first brood is typically one year (one year since birth) [tR = one year since birth], with females generally deferring their first reproductive attempt until the subsequent breeding season after their birth year at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Regarding the species' reproductive output, females produce a clutch of two to five eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = two to five eggs per nesting attempt], and data from long-term monitoring programs indicate that they typically raise a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This yields a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 3.5 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 3.5 offspring per year]. This low annual fecundity is offset by a relatively high adult survival rate.

Respirometry trials conducted on wild-caught individuals at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] have revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of approximately 60.9 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 60.9 milliliters per hour]. This value, derived from oxygen consumption measurements, places the species within the expected range for a passerine of its body mass. Despite this relatively modest metabolic rate, the species exhibits a notable maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 4,343 days [am = approximately 4,343 days], which translates to nearly 11.9 years [am = nearly 11.9 years] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a bird of this size and exceeds that of several closely related alaudid species with similar body masses, suggesting that the Spike-heeled lark employs a conservative energy strategy, likely buffered by the relatively stable and predictable resource base of its semi-arid grassland habitat.
